stories.headline: 'Satluj' controversy explained: CBFC row, OTT takedown and what it means for Diljit Dosanjh
stories.what: The Punjabi film Satluj, associated with Diljit Dosanjh, has become embroiled in a high-profile controversy spanning a CBFC certification dispute and a takedown from OTT platforms. The Times of India has published a full explainer tracing every stage of the row, from the film's clash with the censor board to its removal from streaming. Actor Suvinder Pal Vick has alleged that a deliberate campaign is underway to stop the film, saying the 'game' to block its release is still ongoing.
stories.lens: The Satluj row raises pointed questions about censorship, political pressure on cinema, and the limits of creative freedom for films that tackle sensitive regional subjects.
stories.article:
The Punjabi film Satluj has become one of the most contentious film controversies in recent memory, embroiling Diljit Dosanjh and the film's cast and crew in an escalating battle with the censor board and streaming platforms. The Times of India published a detailed explainer on Friday tracing the full arc of the dispute — from the Central Board of Film Certification's objections to the film's removal from an OTT platform.

Actor Suvinder Pal Vick, who features in the film, has spoken out publicly with pointed language. "Whatever game was being played to stop our film, it is still going on," he told the Times of India, suggesting that opposition to the film goes beyond routine regulatory process. His remarks have only intensified public scrutiny of the case.

The controversy places Satluj alongside a long line of Indian films — including Kamal Haasan's Vishwaroopam and the Netflix film Annapoorani — that have faced withdrawal, bans or platform pull-downs following complaints from various groups. A separate Times of India feature catalogued five such South Indian films, underscoring how recurring these battles between cinema and censorship have become.

For Diljit Dosanjh, one of the most bankable stars in Indian popular culture today, the association with a censored film adds another dimension to his already complex relationship with official institutions. The Satluj case is now being watched closely as a test of how far censor and platform pressure can go in determining what Indian audiences are permitted to see.
key_facts: Satluj faced a CBFC certification dispute and was pulled from OTT
Actor Suvinder Pal Vick alleges a deliberate campaign to block the film
Diljit Dosanjh is associated with the film
Controversy mirrors past cases like Vishwaroopam and Annapoorani

stories.headline: Hema Malini: 'I was never the highest paid actress — got my fee in an envelope, like bhiksha'
stories.what: Veteran actress and politician Hema Malini has revealed that despite her iconic status in Hindi cinema, she was never the highest paid actress of her era. In a candid disclosure, she said her fees were handed to her in an envelope — likening the experience to receiving 'bhiksha' (alms). The remarks, reported by The Indian Express, offer a rare and frank window into the economic realities faced even by top-tier female stars in Bollywood's golden era.
stories.lens: Hema Malini's admission shines a light on the long-standing gender pay gap in Bollywood that predates today's conversations about equity in the film industry.
stories.article:
Hema Malini, one of the most celebrated actresses in Hindi cinema history and a sitting Member of Parliament, has revealed that she was never actually the highest paid actress during her time at the top of Bollywood. In a candid interview carried by The Indian Express, she described receiving her fees in a plain envelope — an experience she compared to being given 'bhiksha', the Hindi and Sanskrit word for alms or charitable giving.

The remark is striking for what it implies: that even at the peak of her stardom, when she was one of the most recognisable faces in Indian popular culture, the financial arrangements around female stars were informal, understated, and bore little relation to the cultural power they wielded. She did not disclose the figures she received, but the nature of the anecdote speaks to a broader systemic devaluation.

For decades, Bollywood's pay structure has been opaque, with male leads commanding significantly larger fees than their female counterparts. Hema Malini's era — spanning the 1960s through the 1980s — saw leading ladies occupy enormous creative space while being compensated far below what their box-office pull arguably warranted.

The comments arrive at a moment when pay parity in Indian cinema remains a live debate, with contemporary actresses including Deepika Padukone and Alia Bhatt having spoken about the subject. Coming from Hema Malini — often called the 'Dream Girl' of Indian cinema — the admission carries particular resonance and historical weight.
key_facts: Hema Malini says she was never Bollywood's highest paid actress
She received her fees in an envelope, comparing it to 'bhiksha' (alms)
The remarks highlight the gender pay gap in Hindi cinema's golden era
